\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\subsection{Compound and Joint Compression}

Combining multiple compression techniques produces non-additive errors.
\cite{spark-aaai2026} report super-additive degradation when combining channel pruning with token eviction, with up to 65\% quality loss exceeding individual component effects---the first explicit measurement of this phenomenon in KV cache sparsity.
\cite{slim-icml2025} formalize compound error for quantization and sparsity, deriving an invertible saliency function for low-rank compensation and confirming that aggregated error is strictly non-additive.
\cite{unicomp-2026} evaluate compound compression across 40+ benchmarks, revealing a consistent \emph{knowledge bias}: reasoning and multilingual capabilities degrade disproportionately relative to factual recall.
The order of compression stages is itself load-bearing: \cite{compression-ordering-2025} show that early quantization causes irreversible information loss, making P$\to$KD$\to$Q strictly preferable.
At a more fundamental level, \cite{phase-transition-compression-2026} characterize independent phase transition points per compression dimension, implying that the joint safe region is the intersection---not the union---of per-dimension safe zones.
On the structural side, the concurrent GRASPrune~\cite{graspune-acl2026} learns global budget-constrained gates to jointly prune FFN channels and attention heads, but treats the pruning decision as static across generation.

These works share a common assumption: compound interaction is either uniform across the generation process or varies only by task.
None examines how the interaction between compression components shifts across reasoning phases within a single generation.

\subsection{KV Cache Eviction Strategies}

Most eviction methods rely on importance scoring, yet accumulating evidence questions its reliability.
\cite{defensivekv-iclr2026} show that standard mean-based importance aggregation is fragile, with worst-case quality loss 2.3--4.3$\times$ higher than expected; their defensive aggregation mitigates but does not eliminate the instability.
\cite{obcache-2025} derive a second-order joint K-V saliency score from optimal brain damage theory, establishing that key pruning impacts quality more than value pruning---a useful asymmetry, though the score remains time-invariant.
\cite{mustafar-neurips2025} achieve 70\% unstructured KV sparsity through per-token magnitude pruning without quality loss, demonstrating that fine-grained sparsity within entries and coarse token eviction are complementary axes.
The concurrent RetentiveKV~\cite{retentivekv-2026} identifies \emph{deferred importance}: tokens with low initial salience can become pivotal later, undermining single-snapshot importance estimates.
\cite{greedy-bias-kvcache-2026} further show that any single importance metric exhibits greedy bias, systematically missing structurally relevant tokens.

A recurring theme is that importance estimates become unreliable under specific conditions.
However, these conditions are characterized in terms of aggregation functions or metric choice---not the reasoning phase during which eviction occurs, nor the interaction with concurrent head pruning.

\subsection{Phase-Aware Inference}

Several concurrent works introduce phase-awareness into LLM inference.
ThinKV~\cite{thinkv-iclr2026} partitions generation into phases and applies different KV cache strategies per phase, achieving strong single-axis results that motivate our phase decomposition---but without compound interaction.
\cite{pagedeviction-eacl2026} manage block-wise eviction with separate prefill and decode policies, a coarse two-phase scheme that does not extend to within-generation reasoning phases.
\cite{decision-repr-transition-2026} discover that layer pruning sensitivity depends on whether a layer operates in the ``silent'' or ``decisive'' phase of representation formation, with silent-phase pruning causing collapse---direct evidence that compression tolerance is phase-modulated.
\cite{doing-more-with-less-2026} provide \emph{sign reversal} evidence: unstructured pruning combined with test-time scaling can exceed unpruned baselines, suggesting that sparsity interacts constructively with extended reasoning under certain conditions.
On the evaluation side, \cite{rac-neurips2025} show that reasoning models exhibit heightened sparsity sensitivity, \cite{raas-acl2025} report non-monotonic token importance across decoding steps, and \cite{sparse-frontier-2025} find no universally optimal sparse attention strategy across tasks and generation stages.

These works establish that inference behavior is phase-dependent and that compression tolerance varies temporally, but they examine either phase-aware compression along a single axis or compound compression without phase conditioning.
Our work bridges this gap: we study how the interaction between head pruning and KV cache eviction \emph{strategy} varies across reasoning phases, revealing a strategy crossover where importance-based eviction outperforms random eviction in high-sparsity phases but underperforms in low-sparsity phases---a compound$\times$phase interaction not predicted by any prior framework.

\cite{obcache-2025} derive a second-order joint K-V saliency score from optimal brain damage theory, establishing that key pruning impacts quality more than value pruning---a useful asymmetry, though the score remains time-invariant.
\cite{mustafar-neurips2025} achieve 70\% unstructured KV sparsity through per-token magnitude pruning without quality loss, demonstrating that fine-grained sparsity within entries and coarse token eviction are complementary axes.
The concurrent RetentiveKV~\cite{retentivekv-2026} identifies \emph{deferred importance}: tokens with low initial salience can become pivotal later, undermining single-snapshot importance estimates.
\cite{greedy-bias-kvcache-2026} further show that any single importance metric exhibits greedy bias, systematically missing structurally relevant tokens.

A recurring theme is that importance estimates become unreliable under specific conditions.
However, these conditions are characterized in terms of aggregation functions or metric choice---not the reasoning phase during which eviction occurs, nor the interaction with concurrent head pruning.

\subsection{Phase-Aware Inference}

Several concurrent works introduce phase-awareness into LLM inference.
ThinKV~\cite{thinkv-iclr2026} partitions generation into phases and applies different KV cache strategies per phase, achieving strong single-axis results that motivate our phase decomposition---but without compound interaction.
\cite{pagedeviction-eacl2026} manage block-wise eviction with separate prefill and decode policies, a coarse two-phase scheme that does not extend to within-generation reasoning phases.
\cite{decision-repr-transition-2026} discover that layer pruning sensitivity depends on whether a layer operates in the ``silent'' or ``decisive'' phase of representation formation, with silent-phase pruning causing collapse---direct evidence that compression tolerance is phase-modulated.
\cite{doing-more-with-less-2026} provide \emph{sign reversal} evidence: unstructured pruning combined with test-time scaling can exceed unpruned baselines, suggesting that sparsity interacts constructively with extended reasoning under certain conditions.
On the evaluation side, \cite{rac-neurips2025} show that reasoning models exhibit heightened sparsity sensitivity, \cite{raas-acl2025} report non-monotonic token importance across decoding steps, and \cite{sparse-frontier-2025} find no universally optimal sparse attention strategy across tasks and generation stages.

These works establish that inference behavior is phase-dependent and that compression tolerance varies temporally, but they examine either phase-aware compression along a single axis or compound compression without phase conditioning.
Our work bridges this gap: we study how the interaction between head pruning and KV cache eviction \emph{strategy} varies across reasoning phases, revealing a strategy crossover where importance-based eviction outperforms random eviction in high-sparsity phases but underperforms in low-sparsity phases---a compound$\times$phase interaction not predicted by any prior framework.
